name: Rice blast (leaf, node and neck blast)
look_for: Spindle-shaped leaf spots with grey or ashy centres and brown edges
Blackened, rotting nodes on the stem
Grey-brown rot at the neck of the panicle, so the panicle bends or falls over, with partly filled or empty grains
not_to_confuse: Brown spot has rounder, smaller brown spots
Sheath blight starts on the leaf sheath near the water line
why_it_happens: It is favoured by high humidity, cool nights, dry nurseries, late planting, crowded plants and too much nitrogen.
act_now: Do not add extra nitrogen. Apply nitrogen in three split doses.
Remove grasses and weeds from the bunds and inside the field.
Drain excess water after heavy rain and avoid very close planting.
Next season avoid dry nurseries and late planting, do not transplant infected seedlings, and ask your KVK for blast-resistant varieties.

options.note: Listed by TNAU for nursery and tillering-stage infection.

when: Do not spray for a few spots. Spray when leaf damage reaches about 2 to 5 percent of the leaf area at tillering or booting.
At flowering and after, spray when leaf damage reaches about 5 percent or when 1 to 2 percent of the necks are infected.
In a bad blast year, 3 to 4 sprays across the nursery, tillering and panicle emergence stages may be needed.
Spray before 11 AM or after 3 PM, not at noon.

precautions: Neck blast cannot be cured once the neck has rotted, so protect the crop before the panicles come out.
Do not spray more often than the label allows.
see_expert_if: The problem keeps spreading after you have treated it once
You are not sure what the problem is
Many panicle necks are already affected

name: Fall armyworm on maize
look_for: Ragged holes and see-through patches on young leaves
Sawdust-like droppings (frass) packed inside the central whorl
Green to brown caterpillars hiding in the whorl, and later feeding on the cob
not_to_confuse: Stem borers cause pin-holes and dead hearts instead of a frass-filled whorl
why_it_happens: Attack can start as early as 14 to 21 days after sowing. The caterpillars hide inside the whorl, where sprays do not reach easily.
act_now: Check plants across the whole field every few days from 2 weeks after sowing, not only at the edges.
Act early. Young plants suffer the most damage.
If only a few plants are affected, ask your KVK about biological or neem-based options.

options.note: Effective in ICAR and university trials.
Effective in ICAR and university trials.
Effective, and also tested as a seed treatment. Ask your KVK.

when: Start when you see fresh whorl damage, and direct the spray into the whorl.
Studies suggest longer-lasting products such as chlorantraniliprole suit the early crop stage, while emamectin benzoate and spinetoram suit about 25 to 40 days after sowing.
Two rounds of spraying may be needed. Spray in the early morning or late afternoon.
Rotate between chemical groups on repeat sprays to slow resistance.

precautions: Follow the waiting period on the label, especially once cobs form.
Check that the product label lists maize and fall armyworm.
see_expert_if: The problem keeps spreading after you have treated it once
You are not sure what the problem is
Damage keeps rising after two sprays

name: Early blight of tomato
look_for: Small dark brown or black leathery spots with rings like a target, on the older leaves first
Spots on stems and on fruit, where they are sunken and often near the stalk end
not_to_confuse: Late blight has water-soaked blotches and whitish fuzz on the underside of leaves
why_it_happens: The fungus survives on infected crop residue and on nightshade weeds, and spreads in humid, wet spells.
act_now: Remove infected lower leaves and destroy them. Do not compost them.
Destroy nightshade weeds and volunteer tomato or potato plants.
Stake the plants for airflow and avoid wetting the leaves. Do not irrigate late in the evening.
Rotate with a crop outside the tomato, potato and brinjal family next season.

when: Start at the first spots. These products protect healthy leaves but do not cure badly infected ones.
Repeat about every 7 to 10 days while the weather stays wet, within the label limit.
Alternate between fungicide groups rather than using one product all season.

precautions: Keep to the waiting period on the label before you pick fruit, and wash the fruit.
see_expert_if: The problem keeps spreading after you have treated it once
You are not sure what the problem is

name: Late blight of tomato
look_for: Small water-soaked patches that grow fast into purple-brown, oily-looking blotches
Grey-white fuzzy growth on the underside of leaves in humid weather
Brown, firm patches on fruit, often at the shoulders
not_to_confuse: Early blight has dry spots with target-like rings
why_it_happens: It appears when humid, cloudy, cool weather lasts for days. Sprinkler irrigation helps it spread.
act_now: Remove badly infected plants early and keep them away from healthy plants.
Remove volunteer tomato and potato plants and nightshade weeds nearby.
Avoid sprinkler irrigation. Check transplants are healthy before planting.

options.note: Used preventively in Indian guidance. Overuse leads to resistance.

when: Spray before the disease reaches you during a cool, humid spell, not after the leaves are dying.
In cool, wet weather extension guidance shortens the interval to about 5 to 7 days, within the label limit.

precautions: Late blight can destroy a field in days, so get expert advice at the first sign.
see_expert_if: The problem keeps spreading after you have treated it once
You are not sure what the problem is
Blotches are spreading to many plants within days

name: Parthenium (congress grass, carrot weed)
look_for: Young plants form a rosette with deeply cut leaves that look like carrot leaves
Mature plants are branched, with many small white flower heads
not_to_confuse: Young plants can be mistaken for carrot or other herb seedlings. Look for the many small white flowers on older plants.
why_it_happens: It spreads by huge numbers of seeds, so the key is to remove it before it flowers.
act_now: Uproot plants before they flower and set seed. This is the most effective method.
Wear thick gloves, long sleeves and a mask. Parthenium can cause skin rash, asthma and eye irritation.
Compost uprooted plants or burn them, and keep animals from eating it.
On wasteland and field boundaries, competitive plants such as Cassia tora or marigold, and the Mexican beetle Zygogramma bicolorata, help. Ask your KVK.

options.note: For non-crop areas such as bunds and wasteland. It kills any green crop it touches.
Used in non-crop areas. It harms broad-leaved crops.
Mentioned by ICAR for use before flowering.

when: Spray before flowering, roughly in the first 7 to 8 weeks after the weed emerges.

Inside a standing crop, ask your agriculture officer which herbicide is registered for your crop. ICAR advice is a crop-safe herbicide about 30 to 35 days after sowing in crops such as maize, sorghum and sugarcane.

precautions: Never spray non-selective herbicide near your crop or in wind. Drift kills crops.
Keep sprayers and runoff away from wells, ponds and streams.
see_expert_if: The problem keeps spreading after you have treated it once
You are not sure what the problem is
It is growing inside your crop and you are unsure what is safe to spray

name: Nutgrass (purple nutsedge, Cyperus rotundus)
look_for: Grass-like plants with shiny dark green leaves and a triangular stem
Small hard tubers (nuts) in chains underground
not_to_confuse: True grasses have round or flattened stems. Sedges like nutgrass have a triangular stem.
why_it_happens: It spreads mainly by underground tubers, so pulling the top growth does not remove it.
act_now: Do deep summer ploughing and repeat it every 3 to 4 weeks, so tubers are brought up to dry and die in the hot sun.
Clear plastic sheeting over moist soil in hot weather (solarisation) kills tubers.
Dense, fast-growing crops and cover crops suppress it. Complete control can take two seasons.
Hand pulling leaves the tubers behind and can make it worse.

options.note: Moves into the tubers. It kills any green crop it touches.
Studied with glyphosate in Indian trials. It harms broad-leaved crops.

when: Spray while the weed is green and actively growing, on fallow land or before sowing.
Expect to repeat. Studies show a single spray rarely kills all the tubers, so combine it with ploughing in summer.
Inside a standing crop, ask your agriculture officer which herbicide is registered for your crop.

precautions: Never spray non-selective herbicide on or near your crop, or in wind.
Keep sprayers and runoff away from wells, ponds and streams.
see_expert_if: The problem keeps spreading after you have treated it once
You are not sure what the problem is
It is spreading through a standing crop
